findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: `owner_id` is interpolated directly into the SQL string with an f-string. Any caller-supplied value containing a single quote breaks out of the string literal, so an attacker who influences `owner_id` can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. `' OR '1'='1` to dump every customer's orders, or a stacked statement on drivers that allow it). Use a parameterized query instead: `query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"` and `cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))` (adjust the placeholder style, e.g. `?`, to the DB driver in use). The fix spans both the query construction and the execute call, so no single-line drop-in is given here.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies owner_id = "x' OR '1'='1"; the f-string produces `WHERE customer_id = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, the cursor executes it, and the function returns every order row in the table to the attacker, exposing all customers' billing data.
findings.title: SQL injection: parameterize the customer_id query

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default `events: list[str] = []` is created once at function-definition time and shared by every call that omits the argument. Each call then appends `event_type` to the same list and returns a copy of it, so events recorded for one shipment (or one tenant/request, in a long-lived server process) are silently returned to unrelated later callers. Beyond being a correctness bug, this is a cross-request data-exposure vector: one caller can observe event types recorded by others. Use a `None` sentinel instead: `def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, list[str]]:` with `if events is None: events = []` at the top of the body.
findings.failure_scenario: In a long-running process, request A calls register_shipment_events("refund_issued"); request B from a different customer later calls register_shipment_events("created") and receives {"created": ["refund_issued", "created"]}, exposing another customer's event history and returning ever-growing, incorrect results.
findings.title: Mutable default argument leaks events across calls

findings.body: The query has no LIMIT and `fetchall()` materializes every matching row, then a second full list of dicts is built on top of it. Memory and latency scale with the owner's entire order history rather than what the caller actually needs. If callers only ever need a bounded slice, add a LIMIT (or paginate); if they truly need everything, iterate the cursor instead of double-materializing with `fetchall()` plus a list comprehension.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer with hundreds of thousands of queued orders triggers this function; the driver buffers the full result set and the comprehension duplicates it as dicts, spiking memory and stalling the request.
findings.title: Bound the order query instead of fetching every row into memory

findings.body: `seen` is a list, so `label in seen` is a linear scan executed once per row, making the whole function O(n"), where n is the number of rows. Track seen labels in a `set` (declare `seen: set[str] = set()` and use `seen.add(label)`) to make each membership check O(1) and the function linear.
findings.failure_scenario: A payment export with tens of thousands of rows makes each row scan the growing `seen` list, turning a millisecond dedup into a multi-second quadratic pass.
findings.title: Use a set for the seen-labels membership check

findings.body: The inner double loop over `zones` and `weights` does not reference `carrier` at all, so the same count is recomputed identically for every carrier, making the function O(carriers x zones x weights) when O(zones x weights + carriers) suffices. Compute the count once before the carrier loop — e.g. `count = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone for weight in weights if weight > 0)` — and assign it to each carrier.
findings.failure_scenario: A tariff cross-check with 500 carriers, 1,000 zones, and 100 weight bands executes 50 million redundant inner iterations instead of 100 thousand plus 500 assignments, stalling the pipeline run.
findings.title: Hoist the zone/weight count out of the carrier loop

findings.body: The docstring promises constant time and explicitly assumes records arrive in chronological order, yet the implementation sorts the whole list, allocating a copy and paying O(n log n) on every call. Under the stated precondition the newest record is simply the last element, so no sort is needed.
findings.failure_scenario: Called on a hot path with a large already-ordered queue, every invocation re-sorts thousands of records, turning an intended O(1) lookup into repeated O(n log n) work and copies.
findings.title: Drop the O(n log n) sort; the input is already chronological

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: `owner_id` is interpolated directly into the SQL string with an f-string, so any value containing a single quote breaks the query, and a crafted value can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. `' OR '1'='1` returns every customer's orders, or a stacked statement mutates data). Pass the value through the driver's parameter binding instead — e.g. `cursor.execute("SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", (owner_id,))` (use `%s` if the driver is psycopg/MySQL-style).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes owner_id = "' OR '1'='1"; the WHERE clause becomes always-true and the function returns order rows for every customer, leaking other customers' billing data.
findings.title: Use a parameterized query instead of interpolating owner_id into SQL

findings.body: `range(1, len(entries))` begins at index 1, so `entries[0]` is never scored and is silently dropped from the ranking. For a single-element list the range is empty and the function always returns `[]` even though one entry exists.
findings.failure_scenario: rank_invoice_entries is called with entries where the first element has the highest score; it is excluded from `scored`, so the returned ranking is missing the top invoice entry, and a one-entry list yields an empty result.
findings.title: Start the range at 0 so the first entry is ranked

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: A mutable default list is created once at function definition time and shared across every call that omits `events`. Because the function mutates it with `events.append(event_type)`, events leak between unrelated calls. If no caller actually passes `events`, the simplest fix is to drop the parameter entirely and return `{event_type: [event_type]}`; otherwise use `events: list[str] | None = None` and initialize `events = [] if events is None else events` inside the body.
findings.failure_scenario: register_shipment_events("picked") is called, then register_shipment_events("shipped") — the second call returns {"shipped": ["picked", "shipped"]}, reporting a stale event from an unrelated shipment, and the shared list grows unboundedly for the process lifetime.
findings.title: Remove the mutable default argument `events: list[str] = []`

findings.body: The condition `weight > 0 and zone` does not reference `carrier`, so every carrier receives exactly the same count — the per-carrier grouping is meaningless. If viability is genuinely carrier-independent, compute the count once outside the loop instead of redoing the O(zones × weights) scan for each carrier; if it should depend on the carrier, the condition is missing that check.
findings.failure_scenario: cross_check_tariff_routes is called with carriers that support different zones; all carriers still report identical counts because the check never consults the carrier, so callers make routing decisions on incorrect per-carrier viability data.
findings.title: Viability check ignores the carrier being counted

findings.body: The docstring promises constant time and states records arrive in chronological order, but the body sorts the whole list — O(n log n) work and allocation on every call. Given the stated ordering assumption, the newest record is simply `records[-1]`; either return that directly or correct the docstring. Note the sort also compares timestamps as strings, which only orders correctly for uniformly formatted values like ISO-8601.
findings.failure_scenario: newest_queue_id is called on a hot path with large record lists expecting the documented O(1) behavior; each call sorts the full list, degrading latency, and if created_at values are not lexicographically ordered timestamps the "newest" id returned is wrong.
findings.title: Sort contradicts the constant-time docstring; use records[-1]

findings.body: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated (Python 3.12+ emits DeprecationWarning, slated for removal) and returns a naive datetime, so the ISO string it produces carries no UTC offset. Downstream consumers parsing `created_at` may interpret it as local time, skewing checkpoint ordering across timezones. Use an aware UTC timestamp instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer in a non-UTC timezone parses the offset-less created_at stamp as local time; checkpoints appear hours off, misordering manifests, and on a future Python release utcnow() is removed and this line raises AttributeError.
findings.title: Replace deprecated utcnow() with a timezone-aware now()

findings.body: The function accepts a `threshold` parameter and its docstring says rows are flagged when they cross "the review threshold", but the comparison hardcodes 5000 and ignores the argument entirely. Either the parameter is dead weight to delete, or — far more likely given the signature — the literal is a bug. The whole function then collapses to `return [row for row in rows if float(row["total"]) > threshold]`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000); rows totaling 1000–5000 silently pass unflagged because the hardcoded 5000 wins, so backorders that should be reviewed are never surfaced.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000

findings.body: `seen` is a list, so `label in seen` is a linear scan and the loop is O(n²) over the input rows. A `set` gives O(1) membership (change `seen.append(label)` to `seen.add(label)` accordingly), or the whole function can be `list(dict.fromkeys(str(row.get("label", "")) for row in rows))` to keep first-seen order.
findings.failure_scenario: unique_payment_labels is called with tens of thousands of payment rows; the quadratic membership scan makes the call take seconds instead of milliseconds, slowing the ledger pipeline.
findings.title: Use a set for seen-label membership checks

findings.body: This whole function is a re-implementation of `sorted(..., reverse=True)`, and the re-implementation introduced a bug: `range(1, len(entries))` starts at index 1, so `entries[0]` is silently dropped from the ranking on every call. Replacing the scored-list scaffolding with a single `sorted()` call is both shorter and correct — delete the `scored` list, the loop, and the `scored.sort(...)` line above.
findings.failure_scenario: rank_invoice_entries is called with entries whose first element has the highest score; the loop never visits index 0, so the top invoice entry is missing from the returned ranking and downstream billing logic processes an incomplete list.
findings.suggestion: return sorted(entries, key=lambda entry: float(entry.get("score", 0)), reverse=True)
findings.title: Collapse to sorted(); the hand-rolled loop also skips the first entry

findings.body: Maintaining parallel `seen` and `labels` lists with an O(n²) `label in seen` membership scan re-implements what `dict.fromkeys()` already does: order-preserving deduplication in one line. Delete the `seen`/`labels` scaffolding and the loop above in favor of the one-liner.
findings.suggestion: return list(dict.fromkeys(str(row.get("label", "")) for row in rows))
findings.title: Replace the two-list dedupe with dict.fromkeys()

findings.body: The inner zone/weight loops never reference `carrier`, so the same count is recomputed once per carrier and every carrier maps to the identical value. The triple-nested loop collapses to computing the count once and fanning it out. If a per-carrier count was intended, the inner condition needs to actually depend on the carrier; as written the extra loops are pure wasted work. Delete the nested loops below when applying this.
findings.suggestion:
count = sum(1 for zone in zones for weight in weights if zone and weight > 0)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Hoist the count out of the carrier loop — it never uses carrier

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: `owner_id` is interpolated directly into the SQL statement with an f-string, so any caller-supplied value becomes part of the query text. A value containing a single quote breaks out of the string literal and lets an attacker append arbitrary SQL (UNION SELECT to read other customers' orders, stacked statements to modify data, etc.). Use the driver's parameter binding instead: build the query as `"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"` (or `?` depending on the DB-API paramstyle) and pass the value via `cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))`. The fix spans both the query construction and the execute call, so no single-line drop-in is given here.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies owner_id = "' OR '1'='1" (or a UNION/stacked-query payload); the f-string embeds it into the WHERE clause, the database executes the injected SQL, and the attacker reads or manipulates every row in the orders table rather than only their own.
findings.title: SQL injection: parameterize the orders query instead of f-string interpolation

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default `events: list[str] = []` is created once at function definition time and shared by every call that omits the argument. Because the function mutates it with `events.append(event_type)`, event types accumulate across unrelated invocations for the lifetime of the process — the returned dict for one shipment will contain event types recorded for other shipments/callers, which is both a correctness bug and an information-bleed between contexts. Change the signature to `events: list[str] | None = None` and initialize `events = [] if events is None else events` inside the body.
findings.failure_scenario: Two independent callers invoke register_shipment_events without passing `events`; the second caller's returned list includes the first caller's event type because both calls mutated the same shared default list, exposing one context's event history to another.
findings.title: Mutable default argument leaks event data across calls

findings.body: This whole function reimplements `sorted()` with an index loop, and the loop starts at `range(1, len(entries))`, so `entries[0]` is silently dropped from the ranking. Collapsing it to a single `sorted()` call both removes the code and fixes the off-by-one.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller ranks a list of invoice entries; the first entry — which may carry the highest score — never appears in the result, so the top invoice is silently omitted from downstream ranking output.
findings.suggestion: return sorted(entries, key=lambda entry: float(entry.get("score", 0)), reverse=True)
findings.title: Replace hand-rolled ranking with sorted(); loop also skips the first entry

findings.body: The inner double loop counts `truthy zones × positive weights`, and that count is identical for every carrier — nothing in the loop body depends on `carrier`. The whole O(carriers × zones × weights) traversal reduces to two `sum()` calls and a dict comprehension. Less code, same result, and no quadratic-plus blowup on large inputs.
findings.failure_scenario: With a few thousand zones, weights, and carriers the function performs billions of redundant iterations to compute a single number repeatedly, stalling the pipeline where one multiplication would do.
findings.suggestion:
count = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone) * sum(1 for weight in weights if weight > 0)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Collapse the triple-nested loop to one multiplication

findings.body: This is a hand-rolled order-preserving dedupe that the standard library does in one expression, and it keeps two identical lists (`seen` and `labels`) while doing O(n) `label in seen` membership checks per row — O(n²) overall. `dict.fromkeys` preserves first-seen order with O(1) lookups.
findings.failure_scenario: On a large rows list (tens of thousands of entries) the linear `label in seen` scan per row makes deduplication quadratic, turning a millisecond operation into seconds.
findings.suggestion: return list(dict.fromkeys(str(row.get("label", "")) for row in rows))
findings.title: Replace the seen/labels loop with dict.fromkeys()

findings.body: The docstring claims constant time and states records arrive in chronological order, yet the body sorts the entire list (O(n log n)) just to read the last element. If the chronological assumption holds, `records[-1]` is the answer with no sort at all; if it doesn't hold, the docstring is wrong. Either way the current code and its contract disagree, and the shorter form deletes the sort.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relying on the documented constant-time behavior invokes this in a hot path over large queues; each call re-sorts the whole list, degrading a supposed O(1) lookup to O(n log n).
findings.suggestion: return str(records[-1].get("id")) if records else None
findings.title: Drop the sort — take the last record directly as the docstring promises

findings.body: The function takes a `threshold` parameter but compares against a hardcoded `5000`, so the caller-supplied value is silently ignored. Either the parameter is dead configurability that should be deleted, or the literal is a bug — given the name and docstring, the comparison should use `threshold`. (Once fixed, the whole function is also a one-line list comprehension: `return [row for row in rows if float(row["total"]) > threshold]`.)
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes threshold=1000 expecting rows above 1000 to be flagged for review; rows totalling 1000–5000 pass unflagged, so oversized backorders skip the review process.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000

findings.body: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime, so the stored `created_at` stamp carries no timezone offset. Using `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` produces an aware timestamp whose ISO string includes `+00:00`, avoiding ambiguity for consumers of the checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: A downstream consumer parses the naive ISO string and interprets it in local time; checkpoints stamped on a UTC-offset host appear hours off, misordering manifest checkpoints — and on Python 3.12+ the call emits a DeprecationWarning ahead of eventual removal.
findings.title: Replace deprecated datetime.utcnow() with a timezone-aware now()

findings.body: The docstring promises constant time and states the records already arrive in chronological order, yet the body sorts the whole list (O(n log n)) just to read the last element. If the chronological-order assumption holds, the sort is code that never needed to be written — the last record is the newest. Either delete the sort or fix the docstring; keeping both is contradictory.
findings.title: Drop the sort; take records[-1] as the docstring assumes

findings.body: The function takes a `threshold: float` parameter but the comparison ignores it and hardcodes 5000, so the knob is dead weight and every caller gets the same cutoff regardless of what they pass. Either wire the parameter into the comparison or delete it — an accepted-but-ignored argument is worse than no argument. (The loop itself is also just `[row for row in rows if float(row["total"]) > threshold]`.)
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000) expecting rows above 1000 to be flagged for review; rows with totals between 1000 and 5000 are silently omitted, so backorders that should be reviewed never surface.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000

findings.body: `seen` and `labels` are maintained as two identical lists — one is pure redundancy — and `label in seen` on a list makes the loop O(n²). Order-preserving deduplication is exactly what `dict.fromkeys` does in one expression, so the whole body is code that never needed to be written.
findings.suggestion: return list(dict.fromkeys(str(row.get("label", "")) for row in rows))
findings.title: Collapse the dedup loop to dict.fromkeys()
